Prep Step 2 — Population analysis

Evaluating and Setting English Learner Exit Thresholds

Sample

Full statewide EL population: every student identified as an English learner (current and former, within the monitoring window), observed across 11 years (2015–2025). Not a single cohort. Never-EL students enter only as the enrollment denominator.

Looking at

Trends over time, grade-level distribution, district variation, entry-grade patterns, and demographic profiles (home language, disability status, alternate-assessment participation, and newcomer vs. long-term EL indicators where the delivery carries them).

Looking for

Two things, not one.

  1. The shape of the EL population in its own right. Where EL students concentrate by grade and district, how large the long-term-EL share is, and how uneven entry patterns are. A reclassification policy technically applies to everyone but lands unevenly: some grades and districts will feel a threshold change far more than others, simply because that is where the EL students are.
  2. The compositional facts that shape the later stages. Heavily K/1 entry, cumulative attrition by grade, and a concentrated long-term-EL presence are what will later justify weighting certain grades’ evidence more cautiously, and analyzing newly arrived and long-term ELs as separate groups rather than one pooled population.

Data coverage

Counts come from the roster only (the base table has rows only where a test happened; the roster is the counting frame). Everything counted here is built on the Overall Composite — the score this state reports as a student’s overall English language proficiency result. The “Annual Overall Composite” column counts student-years with an annual-form result; alternate-form takers are reported as a group and never banded, because their levels are on a different scale.

4. Entry-grade patterns and candidate cohorts

Each student’s entry into EL status is dated from the roster, using the first of the fields in spec$data$entry_sources that is delivered and non-missing (by default LEP_PROGRAM_START_DATE, COHORT_START_YEAR, YEAR_IN_STATUS, then ENTRY_GRADE, which assumes one grade per year). A state’s own count of years in the program maps onto YEAR_IN_STATUS through spec$data$columns$roster; whether that count codes a student’s first year as 1 or as 0 is detected from entrants the panel observes, unless the spec says. A delivered start date reads on the academic calendar (a September date belongs to the next spring year) unless spec$data$entry_date_rule says otherwise. With none of these fields, the panel itself dates entry only when the student first turns current after the panel opens (a student in K in the panel’s first year is also taken as a K entrant that year). A student already EL in the panel’s first year with nothing delivered to date them has an unknown entry: their time in status is a lower bound, and they are excluded from the entry views and from any Check 1 cohort.

On the first observed current year of in-panel entrants, YEAR_IN_STATUS is 1 for 100.0% of them, so it is read as counting the current year (first year = 1) [DERIVED - VERIFY].

Delivered entry fields cover 100.0% of ever-current students. Where the panel also observes the entry (43,640 students first current after 2015), the delivered year matches the first current year for 100.0%; 0 delivered years fell after an observed current year and were pulled back to it.

Left-truncation recomputed here agrees with the delivered LEFT_TRUNCATED flag for 100.0% of students.

Candidate K-start cohorts for Data Check 1 are below. They are the same cohorts Check 1 selects from: membership is the shared cohort derivation, and left-truncated students are excluded by construction.

5. Time in status: new vs. long-term ELs

Years in status count from the entry year resolved in section 4, not from a student’s first appearance in the panel. A student whose entry is unknown (already EL when the panel opened, nothing delivered to date them) has only a lower bound: the years they have been observed as current. Such a student counts as long-term once observed for 6+ years, and is otherwise carried as unknown, which is why the long-term share is reported as a range (at least / at most). The two bounds meet once every student’s entry is dated.

Distributions only. Per the slide-38 guardrail, no mean or average time in status is computed anywhere in this document: a mean of durations across students who entered at different grades, and are censored at different points, describes no one.

6. Initial ELP level

The Overall Composite level at entry, banded per the spec. Only students whose entry is observed inside the panel have an initial level. Alternate-form takers are counted as a group and never banded: the alternate scale is a different measurement scale.

The band recomputed here from the Overall Composite (first annual result at or after entry) agrees with the delivered INITIAL_ELP for 100.0% of the 46,677 entrants carrying both.

Interpreting

This step is not just a technical prerequisite for choosing analytic samples. It is the interpretive backdrop for every Data Check that follows. A grade-level finding, a district pattern, or a subgroup difference in Data Checks 1–4 has to be read through what this step shows: is that grade, district, or subgroup representative of the EL population, or an outlier shaped by unusual entry timing, thin N, or a concentrated long-term-EL presence? Skipped or skimmed, this step lets later results be taken at face value when they actually reflect population idiosyncrasy rather than anything about the exit threshold.

Resist the urge to average

Nothing above averages across groups, and nothing reports a mean time in status. Grade, district, and duration groups are shown as distributions and shares so that the concentration itself stays visible. Keep it that way in the stages that follow.

Additional check — Types 2–6: criteria crosswalk

The exit rule is declared as Type 1 (a single overall composite), so the criteria crosswalk does not apply. criteria_crosswalk, blocked_groups and contested_zone are NULL in the results object. Declare the additional criteria in spec$policy$exit$pathways and set types to activate this check.

Decide before moving on

  • Panel. 11 years (2015–2025).
  • Size. 24,938 current ELs in 2025 (11-year average 22,339).
  • Grade concentration (2025). Grades 2, 3, 1 hold 34.2% of current ELs; K-5 holds 61.3%.
  • Districts (2025). 6 of 12 districts hold two-thirds of current ELs; 0 districts serve fewer than 100.
  • Entry. 62.0% of observed entrants enter in K or grade 1. K-start cohorts that cover the full exit window: 2015 (n = 2,373, 11 years observed); 2016 (n = 2,360, 10 years observed); 2017 (n = 2,411, 9 years observed); 2018 (n = 2,403, 8 years observed); 2019 (n = 2,374, 7 years observed) (plus 6 shorter cohorts, censored at the window’s edge).
  • Time in status (2025). 17.5% of current ELs are in their first year; 25.0% have 6+ years (long-term); entry is unknown for 0.0% (already EL when the panel opened, no entry field delivered).
  • Alternate-form ELP. 0.7% of current ELs in 2025 take the alternate form (reported as a group, never banded).
Decide
  • Which cohorts and subgroups are large and stable enough to analyze reliably? Is there a clean K-start cohort for Data Check 1 (observed at entry, not pandemic-distorted, N well above the suppression floor)?
  • Which grades, districts, or subgroups are most likely to be affected by any eventual policy change and warrant closer attention throughout?
  • Where would a single pooled “all ELs together” analysis obscure more than it reveals? Most notably: newly arrived vs. long-term ELs, and the grades where the long-term share is concentrated.

Spec: SIM. Simulated data, contract 0.4.0. stateELP 0.0.0.9000, run 2026-10-09.
